skill: Diagnosing why adding a second crew does not compress an activity's duration under Fixed Duration & Units/Time
scenario: On a bridge-deck project, activity 'Cure Post-Tensioned Deck Pour – Span 4' has one Concrete Curing Crew assigned at 8h/d, Original Duration 7d, and Duration Type = Fixed Duration & Units/Time. The site team asks whether assigning a second curing crew to the same activity will let it finish in half the time so the pour can be opened to traffic sooner.
question: Will adding a second crew shorten this activity's duration in P6? Explain exactly what recalculates and why, and state whether changing the resourcing here is even the right lever.
explanation: No – under Fixed Duration & Units/Time, both the Duration and each resource's Units/Time (rate) are held constant. Adding a second crew does not shrink Duration; instead total Budgeted Units (labor-hours) doubles, because two crews now work the same fixed 7-day duration at their fixed daily rate. More importantly, curing is a physically time-driven process, not an effort-driven one – concrete needs a fixed number of days to cure regardless of how many crews are standing by, so this Duration Type is actually the correct choice here, and the real answer to the site team is that adding a crew is the wrong lever entirely, not a P6 configuration problem.
reasoning: P6's four duration types define which two of {Duration, Units, Units/Time} stay fixed when the third changes via a resource assignment edit. Fixed Duration & Units/Time locks Duration and the rate; only total Units is free to move, so adding a resource just increases total budgeted effort at the same fixed rate for the same fixed duration – it cannot compress the schedule. Compression is only possible with a duration type where Duration is the dependent variable (e.g., Fixed Units, where total effort is fixed and adding resources increases the combined rate, shortening duration).
commonMistakes: Assuming any added resource in P6 always shortens duration, like a naive effort-driven assumption.
Recommending a Duration Type change to force compression without first checking whether the underlying work is physically time-constrained (curing) rather than effort-constrained.
Confusing Units/Time (a rate) with total Units (total budgeted effort) when explaining what changed.
redFlags: Proposes changing Duration Type purely to make the number the site team wants appear, without evaluating whether the physical process (curing) can actually be compressed by more labor.
p6Checks: Activities view – add the 'Duration Type' column to confirm the activity is set to Fixed Duration & Units/Time before explaining behavior.
Activity's Resources tab – compare Budgeted Units before and after adding the second crew assignment to confirm it doubled while Duration and Units/Time stayed the same.
Only if the work is genuinely effort-driven (e.g., formwork strip-out, not curing), consider switching to Fixed Units so adding a crew increases the combined rate and shortens duration.

skill: Diagnosing a baseline finish variance that stays flat even though the current forecast finish date visibly improved
scenario: On a shopping mall fit-out project, activity 'Install Storefront Glazing – Unit 12' showed Finish Variance – BL Project of -6 working days last month. This month, the activity progressed well and its own current forecast finish date moved 4 days earlier than last month's forecast. Despite that improvement, this month's Finish Variance – BL Project still reads exactly -6 days.
question: Explain the most likely reason the finish variance figure stayed flat even though the current forecast finish genuinely improved by 4 days. What would you check to confirm it?
explanation: Finish Variance – BL Project is calculated as Baseline Finish minus Current Finish. If only the Current Finish moved 4 days earlier and the Baseline Finish were unchanged, the variance would necessarily improve (become less negative) by 4 days. A flat variance despite a genuine current-date improvement is only mathematically consistent with the Baseline Finish reference itself also having moved earlier by roughly the same amount over the same period – most likely because someone updated or reassigned the Project Baseline between the two reporting periods, whether deliberately or in error.
reasoning: Variance columns are only meaningful relative to a fixed reference point. If the reference point (the assigned baseline) is silently replaced or refreshed, period-over-period variance comparisons lose their meaning even though each individual number still calculates correctly at that moment.
commonMistakes: Assuming variance columns always compare against the same original, untouched baseline without verifying it.
Concluding the -6 days must be a data-entry or calculation error rather than checking whether the baseline reference itself changed.
Not checking baseline metadata (creation/last-updated date) as part of routine variance analysis.
redFlags: Reports the flat variance to a client/PM as reassuring stability without investigating why it didn't move as expected.
p6Checks: Project > Maintain Baselines – check the creation date and last-updated timestamp of the currently assigned Project Baseline.
Project > Assign Baselines – confirm which stored baseline is currently assigned as Project Baseline versus what was assigned last period.
Compare the BL Project Finish Date column value for this activity between this period's and last period's exported report to see whether the baseline date itself moved.

followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate moves from diagnosis to a practical process/access-control fix (e.g., restricting who can run Maintain/Assign Baselines).

followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate over-generalizes the paradox rather than recognizing coincidental flatness is also mathematically possible in principle.

skill: Deciding when re-baselining is appropriate versus preserving the original baseline for contractual and claims purposes
scenario: You are the Project Controls Manager on a $180M process plant EPC contract. The project is 5 months behind the original contractual baseline due to a mix of owner-caused design changes and contractor productivity issues, with no formal EOT agreed yet. The Project Director asks you to update (overwrite) the Project Baseline in P6 to match the current schedule so that 'the reports stop looking so red' going forward.
question: How do you respond? What are the risks of resetting the baseline this way, and is there a defensible way to give the Project Director cleaner-looking forward variance without destroying the original record?
explanation: Overwriting the contractual Project Baseline erases the ability to measure cumulative variance against the original commitment – exactly the record needed to support a future EOT claim or defend against liquidated damages – so doing it purely to improve how reports look, with owner-caused delay still in the mix and no agreed EOT, is a serious schedule-integrity and commercial risk. The defensible approach is to preserve the original baseline untouched (rename/archive it clearly, e.g., 'Baseline – Contract [date]') and ADD a new baseline assigned to a different slot (e.g., Secondary, labeled something like 'Baseline – Internal Working [date]') so forward variance can be reported against a realistic recent reference while the original contractual baseline remains intact for entitlement purposes. Any change to what is treated as the CONTRACTUAL baseline should be tied to an actually approved change (an agreed EOT or a revised contract completion date), not an internal reporting preference.
reasoning: Internal performance tracking and contractual entitlement tracking are two different purposes that can legitimately use two different assigned baselines simultaneously (e.g., Primary for contract, Secondary for internal working target); collapsing them into one by overwriting the original baseline sacrifices the contractual record for the sake of internal optics.
commonMistakes: Complying with the request and overwriting the baseline without preserving the original.
Not recognizing the claims/entitlement implication of losing the original baseline record.
Assuming re-baselining is purely a technical, non-commercial decision.
redFlags: Complies without pushback or without preserving history.
Cannot distinguish an internal reporting baseline from the contractual entitlement baseline.
Does not raise that any change to the contractual reference should be tied to an approved change, not a reporting preference.
p6Checks: Project > Maintain Baselines – add a NEW baseline (e.g., 'Baseline – Recovery/Working [date]') rather than overwriting the existing Project Baseline.
Project > Assign Baselines – assign the new baseline to Secondary (or another open slot) while leaving the original Project Baseline assignment untouched.
Confirm whether any proposed baseline change corresponds to an actually approved contract change (EOT/revised completion date) before treating a new baseline as the contractual reference.

skill: Using Primary and Secondary assigned baselines to separate original contractual slippage from recovery-plan performance
scenario: An airport terminal expansion project has its original Project Baseline assigned as Primary, and a client-approved Recovery Schedule (agreed after a 45-day EOT) assigned as Secondary. This period's report shows, for the overall project finish milestone: Finish Variance vs Primary baseline = -62 days; Finish Variance vs Secondary baseline = -9 days.
question: Explain what each of these two variance figures is telling you, and why reporting only one of them to the client would be misleading.
expectedAnswer: The -62 days vs Primary shows total slippage against the ORIGINAL contract baseline, which includes both the already-agreed 45-day EOT and additional slippage that has occurred since. The -9 days vs Secondary isolates current performance against the most recent AGREED commitment (the recovery schedule) only. Reporting only -62 days overstates current underperformance by re-counting the already-excused 45 days as if it were fresh bad news; reporting only -9 days hides the full cumulative picture and understates how far behind the original contract date the project actually still is.
strongAnswer: Notes that both figures should be reported together with clear labeling, since a client or executive audience reading only one number in isolation will draw the wrong conclusion either way.
explanation: Because P6 allows more than one assigned baseline simultaneously, a project can maintain both an original contractual reference and a later approved reference, letting reporting distinguish 'how far behind the contract are we' from 'how are we doing against what we most recently promised'.
reasoning: Variance figures are only interpretable relative to their stated reference point; conflating two different reference points into a single headline number destroys the information needed for both entitlement discussions and forward performance management.
commonMistakes: Reporting only the Secondary (recovery) variance because it looks better, without disclosing the Primary variance.
Assuming the two numbers should reconcile to the 45-day EOT exactly without checking whether the Secondary baseline was formally approved and reflects the full 45 days.

skill: Knowing what a P6 Reflection project is for and how it differs in function from a Baseline
question: What is the primary purpose of creating a 'Reflection' of a project in Primavera P6?

options.label: A
options.text: To create a permanent, non-editable historical snapshot used only for variance reporting

options.label: B
options.text: To create an editable working copy where what-if schedule changes can be tested without affecting the live source project, with accepted changes later merged back

options.label: C
options.text: To generate a PDF snapshot of the current activity layout for distribution

options.label: D
options.text: To duplicate a project permanently into a different EPS node for an unrelated client

explanation: A Reflection is a full, editable copy of a project created specifically so a planner can test schedule changes (what-if scenarios, proposed logic changes, recovery/acceleration options) in isolation from the live schedule, then selectively merge the accepted changes back into the source project using the Merge Reflection into Source Project utility. This is functionally different from a Baseline, which is a static, non-editable snapshot used only for variance comparison and has no merge-back capability.
reasoning: Reflections and Baselines are both 'copies' of a project conceptually, but they serve opposite purposes: a Baseline is meant to stay frozen as a fixed comparison point, while a Reflection is meant to be actively edited and then reconciled back into the live schedule.
commonMistakes: Confusing Reflection with Baseline because both start from a copy of the live project.
Assuming a Reflection is just a report/export rather than a fully functional, schedulable project copy.
p6Checks: Right-click the project in the EPS/Projects window > Add Reflection.
After making and validating edits in the reflection, use the Merge utility to merge accepted changes back into the source project.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Could you achieve the same outcome by just editing the live project directly and undoing changes if you don't like them?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests understanding of why isolation matters on a live, multi-user, actively-progressed schedule.

skill: Distinguishing what can and cannot be accomplished with a Reflection versus a restored Baseline
scenario: A planner wants to test a proposed schedule acceleration (adding weekend shifts to three activities) without disturbing the live, currently-in-progress project schedule the whole team is actively updating. They propose restoring one of the project's existing Baselines as a working file, making the changes there, and then having P6 automatically merge the accepted changes back into the live project.
question: Is this workable using a Baseline the way the planner describes? What is the correct P6 mechanism for this kind of what-if-then-merge workflow, and why does the distinction matter?
expectedAnswer: A restored Baseline can technically be reopened and edited like any ordinary project once restored, but a Baseline has no built-in 'merge back into source' capability – there is no automated utility to reconcile a restored, edited baseline against the live project's current state. The correct tool for this specific what-if-then-merge workflow is a Reflection, which is purpose-built to be edited and then reconciled back into the source project via the Merge Reflection into Source Project utility.
strongAnswer: Notes that restoring and heavily editing a Baseline also risks confusing it with the historical record if it isn't clearly renamed/relocated, since a restored baseline becomes an ordinary project in the EPS with no special protection.
explanation: Baselines and Reflections are both copies, but only Reflections carry the merge-back workflow; using a restored Baseline for this purpose would require manual, activity-by-activity reconciliation with no tool support.
reasoning: P6 deliberately separates the 'frozen comparison record' function (Baseline) from the 'editable what-if with merge-back' function (Reflection) because conflating them would compromise the integrity of the historical baseline record.
commonMistakes: Assuming any copy of a project in P6 can be merged back automatically.
Not recognizing that restoring a Baseline turns it into an ordinary, unprotected project.
redFlags: States that P6 has a generic 'merge any project back' feature not tied to Reflections specifically.
p6Checks: Right-click the project > Add Reflection (not 'Restore' a baseline) for what-if testing intended to merge back later.
Project > Maintain Baselines – note that this dialog offers restore/delete/update, but no merge-back function.
If a baseline is ever restored for other reasons, rename/relocate it clearly in the EPS to avoid confusing it with the live project or an active reflection.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What would you name and where would you place the Reflection in the EPS to avoid confusion with the live project?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests practical project-hygiene awareness, not just conceptual knowledge.

followUpQuestions.prompt: After the reflection is merged, does the reflection project need to be kept?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate knows reflections are typically deleted after a successful merge to avoid EPS clutter and confusion.

dimensions.name: reasoning
dimensions.guidance: Explains why the tools are functionally separated.

dimensions.name: practicalApplication

skill: Handling a Reflection merge safely when the source project has been progressed since the reflection was created
scenario: A planning lead created a Reflection of the live hospital tower project three days ago to test resequencing the MEP overhead rough-in activities. In the meantime, another planner applied the site team's weekly progress update directly to the LIVE source project (not the reflection), moving several actual dates and advancing the Data Date. The lead is now ready to merge the reflection's resequencing changes back into the source project.
question: What is the risk of merging this Reflection now, given the source has changed since it was branched, and what should the lead do to merge safely without losing the intervening progress update?
explanation: Merging a Reflection into a source project that has since changed can create conflicts, because the merge reconciles the reflection's proposed changes against the CURRENT state of the source, activity by activity – if the reflection's own dates/logic are now stale relative to the newer progress update, a careless merge risks overwriting or contradicting the progress that was entered directly into the live project. The safer approach is to first identify what changed in the source since the reflection was branched (e.g., by reviewing the recent progress update log, or comparing the reflection's starting point to the current source using a comparison tool), then either re-create the reflection from the now-current source and redo the resequencing on top of the latest progress, or carefully review the merge utility's proposed change list activity-by-activity before confirming, ensuring the progress update is not clobbered.
reasoning: A Reflection is a point-in-time branch; the longer it lives while the source keeps progressing, the more its own dates diverge from current reality, and the merge tool's reconciliation becomes riskier the larger that divergence is.
commonMistakes: Merging immediately without checking what changed in the source since branching.
Assuming the merge utility automatically and correctly reconciles any conflicting progress data with no review needed.
redFlags: Merges a multi-day-old reflection into an actively-progressed live project without reviewing the change list first.
p6Checks: Before merging, review what changed in the source project since the reflection was created (recent progress update notes, or a comparison against the reflection's starting point).
Use the Merge Reflection into Source Project utility and review the proposed change list carefully before confirming, rather than merging blind.
Consider re-creating the reflection from the now-current source and re-applying the resequencing changes if the source has moved substantially since branching.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What practice would you put in place going forward to reduce this kind of conflict risk on actively-progressed live projects?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate proposes a process fix, such as keeping reflections short-lived or refreshing them regularly.

skill: Using Global Change to mass-reassign a calendar to a filtered subset of activities safely
scenario: A metro rail project discovers that 340 activities across the tunnel boring package were assigned the wrong project calendar (a 5-day-week calendar instead of the correct 6-day-week calendar the TBM crews actually work). Re-assigning each activity manually through the Activities view would be impractical at this scale.
question: Describe how you would use Global Change to correct this efficiently, including how you would limit the change to only the intended activities and verify the result before it affects reporting.
expectedAnswer: Open Global Change, define a change specification that sets the Calendar field to the correct 6-day calendar, restrict the specification to a filtered subset of activities that isolates the tunnel boring package (e.g., by WBS plus the currently-wrong calendar as a condition), run it first in preview/temporary-results mode to review exactly which activities will be affected and how, review that list for correctness, then commit/apply, and finally run Schedule (F9) and review Total Float/critical path for material shifts caused by the calendar change.
strongAnswer: Adds that backing up the project (export XER, or working in a copy/reflection first) before running a mass change at this scale is good practice, given the scope of activities affected.
explanation: Global Change is the correct tool for a rule-based mass edit like this: it lets the change be scoped precisely with a filter, previewed before committing, and applied in one pass instead of hundreds of manual edits.
reasoning: A calendar reassignment of this scale directly changes available working time for 340 activities, which will very likely shift durations, dates, and potentially the critical path itself, so verification after the change is as important as the mechanics of making it.
commonMistakes: Manually editing activities individually instead of using Global Change at this scale.
Applying the change without previewing or scoping the filter tightly, risking touching unrelated activities that happen to share the wrong calendar for a legitimate reason.
Forgetting to re-run Schedule (F9) and check for critical path shifts after the mass calendar change.
redFlags: Applies a mass calendar change with no filter scoping or preview step.
p6Checks: Tools/Enterprise Data > Global Change.
Define the selection using a filter (e.g., WBS = Tunnel Boring Package AND Calendar = [incorrect calendar]) so only intended activities are touched.
Use Global Change's preview/temporary results view to check the affected activity list before committing.
After applying, run Schedule (F9) and review Total Float and the critical path filter for material shifts.

skill: Identifying the checks needed before committing an irreversible Global Change across many activities
scenario: A planner has built a Global Change specification intended to reset the Percent Complete Type to 'Physical' for all incomplete activities across a 2,400-activity offshore platform hook-up and commissioning schedule, ahead of switching the project to physical-percent-complete-based earned value reporting.
question: Before clicking Apply, what would you check first, and why is this particular change higher-risk than a simple text-field update?
expectedAnswer: Check that the filter used truly captures only the intended activities (excluding already-completed activities, milestones, and any Level of Effort activities where Physical % Complete may not be meaningful); run the change in preview/temporary-results mode first and review the affected list and resulting values before committing; back up the project (export XER or snapshot) beforehand since Global Change commits directly to the live project and there is no simple single-click undo across thousands of activities; and recognize that changing Percent Complete Type changes which % field drives Activity % Complete, silently changing progress and EV reporting the moment it's applied, so it should be coordinated with the reporting cycle rather than run mid-period without notice to the wider team.
strongAnswer: Adds that switching the type alone does not populate meaningful physical percentages – a process for the site team to actually maintain Physical % Complete values must already exist or be established alongside this change, or every activity will effectively read 0% or a stale value immediately after the switch.
explanation: This change is higher-risk than a routine data edit because it changes the calculation basis for progress and earned value across the entire schedule at once, and because Global Change commits directly with no built-in safety net beyond restoring from a backup.
reasoning: Percent Complete Type is a control field, not just a data field – it changes which underlying number (Physical, Duration, or Units percent) drives every downstream progress and EV calculation for each activity, so an error in scope or timing has schedule-wide reporting consequences.
commonMistakes: Treating this the same as any routine mass field update without considering its downstream reporting impact.
Not checking whether Physical % values actually exist/are maintained before switching the type.
redFlags: Applies a mass Percent Complete Type change directly to a live, actively-reported project without preview, backup, or team notification.
p6Checks: Global Change dialog – review the filter/selection criteria carefully before applying.
Run in preview/temporary results mode first and review the affected activity list and resulting field values.
Export/back up the project (XER) before applying a mass change of this scope.
After applying, spot-check several activities' Activity % Complete to confirm it now reflects Physical % as intended.

skill: Diagnosing a Global Change that produced unintended blanket results due to a misconfigured conditional rule
scenario: A planner intended a Global Change rule to set the Constraint Type to 'Start On or After' ONLY for activities where Constraint Date was currently blank, using an IF/ISNULL-style condition. After running it, they discover that activities that already had a different constraint type and date, entered deliberately by the project team, were also overwritten.
question: What is the most likely cause of this over-broad result, and how would you recover and prevent it from happening again?
explanation: The most likely cause is that the conditional test was written against the wrong field or mismatched the intended logic – for example, testing whether Constraint Type was blank rather than Constraint Date, or having the IF/ISNULL condition and the THEN field assignment reference different, inconsistent fields – so the condition evaluated true for activities it should have excluded, and the THEN clause overwrote their existing, intentional constraints. Recovery requires restoring from a pre-change backup/export, since Global Change commits directly to the live project and there is no single 'undo' for a mass change that has already been applied and saved; manually reversing thousands of edits by hand is impractical and error-prone. The corrected rule should then be re-tested in preview/temporary mode against a small, clearly-bounded filtered subset before being applied to the full activity population again.
reasoning: Global Change rules are only as safe as the precision of their IF/THEN logic; a mismatch between the field tested and the field acted on is a classic cause of a rule silently applying far more broadly than intended.
commonMistakes: Trusting the rule's logic conceptually without testing it on a small sample first.
Attempting to manually reverse the damage activity-by-activity instead of restoring from backup.
Not re-verifying the corrected rule in preview mode before reapplying it broadly.
redFlags: Proposes manually fixing thousands of overwritten activities by hand rather than restoring from backup.
Reapplies a 'corrected' rule directly to the full population without re-testing on a small sample first.
p6Checks: Global Change specification editor – review exactly which field the IF condition tests (Constraint Date vs Constraint Type) versus which field the THEN clause sets.
Restore the project from the pre-change backup/XER export if one exists.
Re-test the corrected rule in preview/temporary mode against a small filtered subset before applying it to the full population again.

skill: Diagnosing why a mixed AND/OR filter returns unexpected results because P6's Filters dialog has no nested grouping
scenario: A planner on an industrial fit-out project builds a filter intending to show '(Critical activities OR activities with Total Float <= 5 days) AND assigned to the Electrical subcontractor.' The filter rows, as built, are: Row 1 = Total Float is <= 0; Row 2 = Or, Total Float is <= 5; Row 3 = And, Responsibility Code is Electrical. After applying it, Electrical activities with 40+ days of float show up in the results, which shouldn't be possible under the intended logic.
question: What is the most likely structural reason this mixed AND/OR filter produces results outside the intended logic, and how would you rebuild it to reliably get exactly the intended set?
explanation: P6's standard Filters dialog evaluates all condition rows as a single flat sequential list using each row's individual And/Or join operator – it has no capability to nest or parenthesize conditions the way a query language would. An intended grouping like '(A OR B) AND C' cannot be expressed reliably as three simple rows with per-row And/Or joins, because the result depends on how P6 evaluates the flat sequence, not on the grouping the planner had in mind. The safest fix is to simplify the logic rather than fight the tool: since every Critical activity (Total Float <= 0) is already a subset of Total Float <= 5, the OR condition is redundant, and the filter can be rebuilt as a simple two-row AND-only filter (Total Float <= 5 AND Responsibility = Electrical), which expresses the same intended set unambiguously.
reasoning: Once a filter genuinely needs true mixed AND/OR logic with more than one grouping, the flat-list structure of P6's Filters dialog cannot express it directly and reliably; recognizing when a condition can be algebraically simplified to avoid the mix (as here) or splitting the work into two sequential filtering/review passes are the two safe workarounds.
commonMistakes: Assuming the row order and And/Or labels always produce standard mathematical AND/OR precedence.
Not noticing the OR condition was logically redundant given the AND condition would already be checked next.
Building complex mixed-logic filters without testing the result against a few known activities.
redFlags: Insists the filter dialog supports parenthetical grouping and searches for a nonexistent feature instead of simplifying the logic.
p6Checks: Edit > Filters (or the Filters bar) – review each condition row's join operator (And/Or) in sequence, top to bottom.
Test the rebuilt filter against a few known activities (one that should pass, one that should fail) to confirm it behaves as intended.

Where logic is genuinely complex and can't be simplified, apply filters in two sequential steps (filter by one condition, review, then manually assess the second) rather than relying on ambiguous mixed rows.

explanation: Group and Sort By supports multiple nested grouping bands with per-band summary rows, which is exactly what a two-level WBS-then-responsibility reporting layout requires, but the summary function per column needs a deliberate check rather than blind acceptance of the default.
reasoning: The grouping structure organizes rows; the column configuration and summary function determine whether the subtotal rows communicate anything useful to a project manager reading the meeting output.

Adding the grouping bands but not the underlying columns, so no summary values actually display.

skill: Knowing what Resource Leveling in P6 actually changes to resolve over-allocation
question: When you run Level Resources in P6 on an over-allocated schedule, what does the leveling process actually do to resolve the over-allocation?

options.label: A
options.text: It deletes or reduces resource assignments until the resource is no longer over-allocated

options.label: B
options.text: It delays the start of lower-priority activities, within available float or beyond it if that option is enabled, so competing demand for the same resource no longer overlaps

options.label: C
options.text: It automatically increases the resource's Max Units/Time to cover the shortfall

options.label: D
options.text: It changes each affected activity's Duration Type to Fixed Units so durations compress automatically

explanation: Leveling is a heuristic that resolves resource over-allocation by delaying activities according to a leveling priority order, not by altering relationships, resource quantities, or Duration Type. It can be constrained to only delay within existing Total Float, or allowed to push activities (and potentially the project finish) beyond their float if that option is enabled.
reasoning: Leveling operates on top of the already-calculated CPM schedule; it inserts leveling delays to sequence competing resource demand, it does not change the underlying logic or resourcing data.
commonMistakes: Believing leveling adjusts resource quantities or availability automatically.
Believing leveling changes activity logic or Duration Type.
p6Checks: Tools > Level Resources (or the Level toolbar icon) – review the Leveling Priorities list and the 'Level resources only within activity Total Float' option before running.
Resource Usage Profile/Spreadsheet – check for over-allocation before and after leveling to confirm the result.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Can leveling change the project's Total Float basis for reporting purposes?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate understands leveled dates and pure CPM float are not automatically the same reporting basis.

skill: Setting a sensible leveling priority order to protect the true critical path during resource leveling
scenario: On a data center campus build, three activities compete for the same specialist commissioning engineer in the same week: 'Commission UPS System' (0 days Total Float, on the critical path), 'Commission BMS Integration' (12 days Total Float), and 'Punch List Walkdown – Building B' (25 days Total Float). Leveling is about to be run for the first time on this schedule.
question: How would you set up the leveling priority so the leveling result does not delay the truly critical activity, and what would you verify in P6 after running Level Resources to confirm it worked as intended?
expectedAnswer: Order the leveling priority so lower-Total-Float activities are favored ahead of higher-float ones when there is a resource conflict – in practice, sorting/prioritizing by Total Float ascending (or explicitly setting the Leveling Priority field on 'Commission UPS System' to a higher priority) so the leveling engine delays 'Punch List Walkdown' and/or 'Commission BMS Integration' first, not the critical activity. After running Level Resources, check that 'Commission UPS System' still shows 0 days Total Float and its dates did not move, while the higher-float activities absorbed the delay instead.
strongAnswer: Notes that leveling within float generally protects the critical path only if 'Level resources only within activity Total Float' is enabled and the priorities are sound; if 'level beyond float' is allowed and demand genuinely cannot be resolved within the available float, even the critical activity could be delayed and the project finish could slip, so the leveling report should be reviewed after every run, not just trusted based on the priority setup.
explanation: P6's leveling engine resolves conflicts using the leveling priority order combined with the within-float constraint; deliberately ordering priority to favor low-float/critical work is the standard way to protect the driving path during leveling.
reasoning: Without a deliberate priority setup, leveling may default to an order (such as Activity ID or Early Start) that does not account for float, risking delay of the truly critical activity purely because of list order or naming.
commonMistakes: Leaving leveling priority at its default without reviewing whether it favors low-float activities.
Assuming 'within float' leveling automatically protects the critical path regardless of priority order.
Not checking the leveling report/log after running to confirm which activities actually moved.
redFlags: Runs leveling without reviewing the priority list or the 'within float' setting at all on a schedule with a genuinely critical activity in the conflict set.
p6Checks: Tools > Level Resources dialog – review/adjust the Leveling Priorities list (by Total Float and/or the Leveling Priority field) before running.
Confirm 'Level resources only within activity Total Float' is checked, given the intent to protect the critical activity.
After leveling, check 'Commission UPS System' Total Float and dates are unchanged, and review the Leveling report/log for which activities were actually delayed.

subcategory: Resource Leveling – Beyond Float / Project Slip
skill: Diagnosing an unexpected project finish date slip caused by resource leveling running beyond available float
scenario: A planner runs Level Resources on a wind farm construction schedule to resolve an over-allocated heavy-crane crew. After leveling, the project finish date has moved out by 11 days, even though the pre-leveling CPM schedule (before leveling) showed the same finish date, with 0 days float on the driving path, and no logic or calendar changes were made by anyone.
question: What is the most likely reason leveling alone moved the project finish date, and how would you confirm the cause and correct it if this delay is not acceptable to the project?
explanation: The most likely cause is that resource demand for the crane crew genuinely could not be resolved within the float available on the competing activities, and leveling was allowed to push activities – including some on or near the critical path – beyond their available float in order to resolve the over-allocation, extending the calculated finish date. This is expected leveling behavior when demand exceeds what float alone can absorb; it is not a logic or calendar error. To confirm, review the Leveling report/log for which activities were delayed and by how much, and check whether 'Level resources only within activity Total Float' was enabled for this run. To correct it if the 11-day slip is unacceptable, options include adding a second crane/crew to relieve the demand conflict, resequencing so competing crane-dependent activities overlap less, or formally reporting and accepting the resource-driven finish date as distinct from (and later than) the pure logic-driven finish date, since the two can legitimately differ.
reasoning: Leveling delays are inserted on top of the CPM-calculated schedule specifically to resolve resource conflicts; when the conflict cannot be absorbed within existing float, the only ways leveling can resolve it are to extend the schedule (if allowed to go beyond float) or leave the over-allocation unresolved (if constrained to stay within float).
commonMistakes: Assuming a finish-date slip after leveling must indicate a logic or calendar error, since 'nothing else changed'.
Not checking whether the leveling run allowed activities to move beyond their available float.
Treating the leveled finish date and the pure CPM finish date as if they were always the same number.
redFlags: Reports the leveled 11-day slip to the client as a pure schedule delay without explaining it originated from resource leveling, not logic.
p6Checks: Tools > Level Resources dialog – check whether 'Level resources only within activity Total Float' was enabled for this run.
Review the Leveling report/log to see exactly which activities were delayed and by how much.
Compare the pre-leveling (pure CPM) finish date to the post-leveling finish date and clearly label/report both if the difference is material.
Resource Usage Profile – confirm the crane crew's over-allocation is actually resolved after leveling.

skill: Correctly identifying which assigned resource's calendar drives a Resource Dependent activity's duration when multiple resources with different calendars are assigned
scenario: Activity 'Test & Commission Switchgear – Substation 3' is set to Activity Type = Resource Dependent, with two resources assigned for the full duration: a specialist commissioning engineer working a 5-day/week calendar, and an OEM technician working a 6-day/week calendar.
question: Given the Resource Dependent activity type, whose calendar actually drives this activity's calculated duration, and what mistake would a candidate make by assuming P6 automatically uses whichever resource's calendar is more restrictive?
expectedAnswer: P6 does not automatically average or select the most-restrictive resource's calendar for a Resource Dependent activity. Exactly one assigned resource is flagged as the 'Driving' resource on the Resources tab, and it is that resource's calendar (and rate) that determines the activity's calculated duration; the other assigned resource works alongside it but does not, by itself, change the calculated duration. So the real answer depends entirely on which of the two resources is marked Driving on this specific assignment, not on some automatic 'most restrictive wins' rule.
strongAnswer: Notes the practical risk: if the 6-day technician is marked Driving while the 5-day engineer is actually the real-world bottleneck, the calculated duration will understate the true elapsed time needed, and the schedule will silently be optimistic until this is caught.
expertAnswer: Adds that this should be checked explicitly on commissioning-heavy schedules with mixed-calendar specialist resources, since misidentifying the driving resource across many such activities can compound into a materially optimistic overall schedule without any single obviously wrong data point to flag it.
explanation: Resource Dependent activities calculate duration from a single 'Driving' resource's calendar and rate, not from an automatic comparison of all assigned resources' calendars; this is also what distinguishes Resource Dependent from Task Dependent, where the activity's own assigned calendar governs regardless of resource calendars.
reasoning: The Driving resource concept exists precisely so P6 has one deterministic calendar/rate to calculate duration from when multiple resources are assigned; verifying which resource holds that flag is the only reliable way to know which calendar actually governs.
commonMistakes: Assuming P6 automatically uses whichever assigned resource's calendar is most restrictive.
Not checking which resource is flagged 'Driving' before predicting duration behavior.
Confusing Resource Dependent (a resource's own calendar can drive the calculation) with Task Dependent (the activity's own calendar drives it regardless of resource calendars).
redFlags: States with confidence that P6 automatically compares all assigned resources' calendars and uses the most restrictive one.
p6Checks: Activity's General/Status tab – confirm Activity Type is Resource Dependent.
Resources tab – check the 'Driving' flag on each assignment to see which resource actually governs the calculated duration.
Compare each assigned resource's calendar (5-day vs 6-day) against which one is marked Driving to assess whether the calculated duration is realistic.
If the wrong resource is Driving, correct the flag and re-verify the recalculated duration.

skill: Explaining how a Level of Effort activity's duration is derived and why it cannot independently drive the critical path
scenario: A project controls lead configured 'Site Safety Supervision' as a Level of Effort (LOE) activity spanning the entire earthworks package, tied via Start-to-Start to the first earthworks activity and Finish-to-Finish to the last. A junior planner is confused because the LOE activity's Total Float always seems to mirror whatever is happening on the underlying earthworks activities, and asks whether the LOE activity itself could ever become the driving/critical activity that determines the project finish date.
question: Can a Level of Effort activity independently become the driving activity that determines the project finish date? Explain how its duration and dates are actually determined.
expectedAnswer: No. An LOE activity has no independent duration logic of its own; its start and finish, and therefore its duration, are derived entirely from the span of the activities it is tied to – here, from the earliest start of the first earthworks activity to the latest finish of the last. It mirrors that span rather than imposing a constraint back onto it, so it cannot itself become the activity that drives the project finish date; it is a dependent, reporting-style activity, not a schedule-driving one.
strongAnswer: Notes that the LOE activity's Total Float typically reflects the float of whichever underlying activity currently governs its span, which explains the junior planner's observation directly, and that this is expected, correct behavior rather than a data problem worth 'fixing'.
explanation: LOE duration is calculated automatically from its tied predecessor/successor span rather than through independent CPM logic, so it cannot be a driving activity in the CPM sense even though it can show 0 days Total Float when its governing span happens to be critical.
reasoning: Because P6 recalculates the LOE's span to match its tied activities every time the schedule runs, any apparent 'criticality' of the LOE activity is a reflection of the underlying activities' criticality, not an independent driving effect.
commonMistakes: Treating an LOE activity showing 0 days Total Float as evidence that the LOE itself is driving the schedule.
Assuming LOE duration is entered/estimated like a normal activity rather than derived from its tied span.
redFlags: Cannot explain that LOE duration is a derived, not an independently logic-driven, quantity.
p6Checks: Activity's General tab – confirm Activity Type = Level of Effort.
Relationships tab – confirm the SS/FF ties that actually define the LOE's span.
Compare the LOE activity's Total Float against the Total Float of whichever earthworks activity currently governs its start or finish, to confirm it is mirroring rather than driving.

followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests understanding that LOE recalculates its span every schedule run rather than holding a fixed duration.

skill: Identifying resource over-allocation in P6 before issuing a look-ahead schedule
scenario: You are about to issue a 6-month look-ahead schedule for a warehouse automation retrofit and want to confirm no single resource, labor or equipment, is over-committed across concurrent activities before issuing it.
question: What would you check first in P6 to identify resource over-allocation across this look-ahead window?
expectedAnswer: Open the Resource Usage Profile (or Resource Usage Spreadsheet) for the relevant resources, set the timescale to cover the look-ahead window, and compare the plotted demand (units/time) against each resource's Max Units/Time (availability limit) – any period where demand exceeds that limit line is an over-allocation.
strongAnswer: Adds using the Resource Assignments view grouped by resource as a secondary check to scan for overlapping high-demand periods activity by activity, especially for resources not showing a clean profile.
explanation: The Resource Usage Profile is purpose-built to visualize demand against availability over time, which is exactly the comparison needed to catch over-allocation before it becomes a live scheduling problem.
reasoning: Over-allocation is inherently a time-phased comparison (demand vs. availability across a calendar), which a single-activity view cannot show; the Profile/Spreadsheet view is designed specifically to reveal this.
commonMistakes: Only reviewing individual activities' resource assignments without checking the time-phased aggregate demand.
Not setting Max Units/Time correctly on the resource, making the over-allocation comparison meaningless.
p6Checks: View > Resource Usage Profile (or Spreadsheet) – filter/select the relevant resources.
Compare plotted demand against each resource's Max Units/Time (Resource Details > Limits tab).
Cross-check with the Resource Assignments view grouped by resource for a second look at overlapping periods.

skill: Explaining why leveled activity float should not automatically be reported as the schedule's authoritative CPM float basis
scenario: On a petrochemical turnaround schedule, after running Level Resources, activity 'Replace Heat Exchanger Bundle – E-204' shows a Start date 6 calendar days later than its logic-calculated (unleveled) early start, and its displayed Total Float dropped from 8 days to 2 days in the leveled view. A project engineer argues this proves the true schedule risk on this activity increased and wants to report the 2-day figure to the client as the activity's real Total Float.
question: Is reporting the leveled 2-day float as the activity's 'real' Total Float technically correct? Explain what leveling changed versus what CPM logic actually says, and what you would check before accepting the project engineer's conclusion.
explanation: Leveling delays activities to resolve resource conflicts by inserting a leveling delay on top of the CPM-calculated schedule; it is a resource-driven heuristic, not a recalculation of the underlying logic. Whether the displayed float after leveling reflects a genuine increase in logic-driven risk, or is partly an artifact of the leveling delay itself consuming float, depends on how the leveling run was configured (for example, whether early/late dates were preserved for float-calculation purposes versus recalculated against the leveled dates). Before accepting the project engineer's conclusion, compare the pure CPM (unleveled) Total Float against the leveled figure, check the leveling options used for this run, and confirm which basis – leveled or unleveled – the project actually uses for contractual float and critical path reporting, since conflating the two without disclosure risks materially misrepresenting schedule risk to the client in either direction.
reasoning: Total Float in an unleveled CPM run is a pure function of logic, durations, calendars, and constraints. Once leveling delays are introduced, a float figure read directly off the leveled schedule reflects both the underlying logic AND the leveling heuristic's delay decisions, which is a different and less standardized basis than pure CPM float; treating the two as interchangeable without qualification is a common but technically imprecise practice that can distort risk reporting.
commonMistakes: Treating leveled float and CPM (logic-only) float as identical in meaning.
Not checking which leveling option was used before interpreting a post-leveling float change.
Assuming any float drop after leveling automatically signals a genuine increase in schedule risk rather than partly reflecting a leveling artifact.
redFlags: Reports leveled float to a client as the schedule's contractual float basis without disclosing that resource leveling was applied.
Cannot articulate any difference between leveled and unleveled float.

skill: Predicting how applying a front-loaded resource curve changes the shape of the cumulative Planned Value S-curve without changing total budget
scenario: Activity 'Procure & Deliver Precast Facade Panels' has a resource assignment with Budgeted Cost of $2,400,000 spread by default in a flat, linear distribution across its 20-week duration. The cost engineer applies a predefined 'Front Loaded' resource curve to the assignment instead.
question: What changes and what stays the same after applying the Front Loaded curve? How would this affect the shape of the project's cumulative Planned Value (PV) S-curve if several major assignments are curved this way?
expectedAnswer: Total Budgeted Cost for the assignment stays $2,400,000 – the curve only changes HOW that fixed total is distributed across the 20-week duration, weighting more of it toward the earlier weeks and less toward the later weeks instead of the flat per-week amount a default linear distribution produces. Applied across several major assignments, this shifts the cumulative PV S-curve to rise more steeply early and flatten out later, rather than the smoother, more even S-shape a linear distribution would produce.
strongAnswer: Notes the curve should reflect a genuine planned spending/production profile (e.g., an early procurement- and mobilization-heavy cost pattern) rather than being applied cosmetically to make early PV look larger; using it without a real basis distorts later EV-versus-actual-cost comparisons.
explanation: Resource/cost curves in P6 redistribute a fixed budgeted total non-linearly over an assignment's duration; they never change the total, only the period-by-period allocation used to build PV.
reasoning: PV is built up from the time-phased budgeted cost of every resource assignment; if several large assignments are all weighted early via curves, the aggregate cumulative PV curve necessarily reflects that same early weighting.
commonMistakes: Assuming a curve changes the total budgeted cost of the assignment.
Not checking whether the curve reflects a genuine planned profile versus being applied for a more favorable-looking early PV.
redFlags: Applies front-loaded curves broadly with no operational basis, purely to move PV earlier in the schedule for reporting optics.

skill: Diagnosing an earned-value distortion caused by an inconsistent mix of Percent Complete Types across a resource-loaded schedule
scenario: On a rail electrification project, Earned Value is calculated in P6 based on each activity's Percent Complete Type. A schedule audit finds: 60% of budget-weighted activities use Duration % Complete, calculated as (Original Duration - Remaining Duration) / Original Duration; 30% use Units % Complete; and 10% use Physical % Complete entered manually by site engineers. The project's overall SPI has read suspiciously close to 1.00 every month for the past year, even through a period the client independently confirms was a serious slippage.
question: How could an inconsistent, budget-weighted mix of Percent Complete Types across the schedule contribute to an EV signal (SPI near 1.00) that doesn't reflect real performance? What would you check first?
explanation: Duration % Complete is calculated purely from Remaining Duration entries, which planners can update mechanically (e.g., decrementing remaining duration in line with elapsed calendar time each period as a matter of habit) rather than tying it to independently verified physical output. If 60% of the schedule's budget-weighted earned value is effectively driven by this potentially superficial, duration-based self-reporting rather than the more defensible Units or Physical percent types, SPI can track suspiciously smoothly near 1.00 without genuinely reflecting field reality – especially if Remaining Duration is habitually decremented by roughly the elapsed period regardless of true progress.
reasoning: Percent Complete Type controls the source of truth for Activity % Complete on a per-activity basis; when the dominant, highest-budget-weight type is one prone to mechanical rather than evidence-based updates, the aggregate EV signal inherits that weakness even while individual numbers all calculate correctly.
commonMistakes: Assuming SPI near 1.00 is inherently good news without checking the quality of the underlying percent-complete data feeding it.
Treating all three Percent Complete Types as equally reliable indicators of physical progress.
Not checking whether Remaining Duration entries correlate with elapsed time rather than field-verified progress.
redFlags: Accepts a suspiciously smooth SPI trend at face value without ever cross-checking against an independent progress source.
p6Checks: Activities view – add 'Percent Complete Type' as a column and group by it to see the budget-weighted split across the three types.

subcategory: Cost Loading – Cost Accounts vs Resource Assignments
skill: Distinguishing what a Cost Account organizes versus what a resource/role assignment's Budgeted Cost represents
question: In P6, what is the main functional difference between a 'Cost Account' and a resource or role assignment's 'Budgeted Cost'?

options.label: A
options.text: Cost Account is a hierarchical categorization/coding structure used to group and roll up costs (e.g., by discipline or cost type) for reporting; Budgeted Cost is the actual dollar amount tied to a specific resource or role assignment on an activity

options.label: B
options.text: Cost Account is used only for labor costs, while Budgeted Cost is used only for material costs

options.label: C
options.text: Cost Account and Budgeted Cost are simply two different names for the same field

options.label: D
options.text: Assigning a Cost Account removes the need to assign a resource or role to the activity

explanation: Cost Accounts are a hierarchical enterprise coding structure (e.g., by discipline, cost type, or WBS-like breakdown) that assignments and expenses can be tagged with, allowing costs to be rolled up and reported by that structure independently of the WBS or activity codes. Budgeted Cost is the actual dollar figure produced by a resource's or role's rate x units (or a manually entered expense), the number a Cost Account then helps organize and report.
reasoning: A Cost Account without any assignments tagged to it holds no cost by itself; it is purely an organizing dimension, whereas Budgeted Cost is the underlying data being organized.
commonMistakes: Believing a Cost Account itself carries a budget value independent of assignments.
Confusing Cost Accounts with WBS, which is a different, project-specific hierarchical breakdown.

skill: Using Claim Digger to isolate logic, duration, and constraint changes between two schedule submissions before drafting a delay narrative
scenario: A contractor's monthly schedule update (Update 14, this period's data date) shows the project finish date has slipped 22 calendar days versus Update 13 (last month's data date) – the largest single-month slip on the project so far. Before drafting any delay narrative or issuing a notice, the delay analyst wants to isolate exactly what changed between the two XER submissions, not just observe the resulting date difference.
question: How would Claim Digger help here, and what categories of change would you specifically want it to surface before concluding what caused the 22-day slip?
explanation: Claim Digger, accessed via Tools > Claim Digger in P6 Professional, compares two P6 schedules (or two dated XER versions of the same project) and produces a structured report of differences at the header, activity, and relationship level, including added/deleted activities, duration changes, added/deleted/modified relationships (including lag and relationship type changes), constraint changes, and calendar changes. Before concluding what caused the 22-day slip, the analyst would want Claim Digger to surface any new or deleted logic between the two updates, duration changes on activities (especially those on or near the critical path), constraint changes (a new or shifted finish constraint can move the finish date without any duration change at all), and calendar reassignments – any of which could explain part or all of the 22 days independently of genuine field progress slippage.

commonMistakes: Drafting a delay narrative directly from the finish-date difference without first isolating what actually changed.
Assuming Claim Digger's output automatically identifies the cause rather than just listing the raw differences requiring further analysis.
Not cross-referencing flagged changes against the driving path to confirm they actually affected the finish date.
redFlags: Attributes the full 22-day slip to field progress without first ruling out logic, constraint, or calendar changes.

Review the Activities tab of the Claim Digger report for duration and constraint changes.

subcategory: Multiple Projects – Ignore Relationships to and from Other Projects
skill: Diagnosing a critical path discrepancy caused by scheduling a single project in isolation versus with all cross-project relationships honored
scenario: A program consists of three linked P6 projects in the same EPS: 'Enabling Works,' 'Main Structure,' and 'MEP Fit-Out,' connected by cross-project relationships (e.g., an external Finish-to-Start from Enabling Works into Main Structure). When 'Main Structure' is opened and scheduled ALONE, its own finish milestone shows 14 days of Total Float. When all three projects are opened TOGETHER and scheduled, the same milestone shows -6 days of Total Float.
question: What is the most likely reason the same activity's Total Float differs so dramatically depending on how the projects were opened for scheduling, and which figure should the planning team treat as authoritative for reporting?
explanation: The most likely reason is that when 'Main Structure' is scheduled alone, cross-project relationships to and from Enabling Works and MEP Fit-Out are not being honored in the calculation, whether because 'Ignore relationships to and from other projects' is enabled or simply because the other projects are not open for P6 to span outward into, so its float is calculated as if it were an isolated project. When all three are open together with that option disabled, the real driving constraint from a delayed Enabling Works predecessor is honored, revealing the true -6 days of Total Float. The figure calculated with all genuinely linked projects open together and cross-project relationships honored is the one that reflects the program's real logic and should be treated as authoritative for reporting, since the single-project run was calculating float against an artificially incomplete logic network.
reasoning: Total Float depends on the complete set of logic constraining an activity's late dates; if part of that logic (an external predecessor from another project) is excluded from the calculation, the resulting float number describes a hypothetical isolated project, not the real program.
commonMistakes: Assuming the standalone-project float figure is simply more conservative or safer to report.
Not checking the 'Ignore relationships to and from other projects' option before comparing float results between single- and multi-project scheduling runs.
Treating the two figures as equally valid alternative views rather than recognizing one is calculated against incomplete logic.
redFlags: Reports the more favorable 14-day float figure without checking why it differs so much from the multi-project result.

Confirm whether all logically linked projects (Enabling Works, Main Structure, MEP Fit-Out) were open together when the -6 days figure was calculated.

Establish and document a standard practice for which set of projects must be open together before any float or critical path figure is reported.

skill: Explaining how scheduling multiple open projects together versus individually changes calculated critical path and float results at the program level
scenario: A joint venture partner insists on scheduling and reporting each of the program's four sub-projects independently every month, arguing 'each contractor is only responsible for their own project.' The planning manager on the client side is concerned this practice understates program-level schedule risk.
question: Is the JV partner's independent-scheduling practice likely to produce an accurate picture of program-level critical path and float? Explain the mechanism, describe what you would recommend instead, and note any legitimate reason the JV partner's approach might still make sense for some purposes.
explanation: Scheduling each sub-project independently only calculates float and critical path relative to that sub-project's own constraints and calendar; any cross-project (external) relationships to other sub-projects are either ignored or effectively replaced by a substitute constraint, which can materially understate float consumption and hide a program-level critical path that actually threads through multiple sub-projects. The planning manager should recommend periodically opening and scheduling ALL logically linked sub-projects together, with cross-project relationships honored, to calculate and report the true program-level critical path and float, alongside whatever standalone reporting the JV partner wants to keep for their own internal purposes. There is a legitimate reason for the JV partner's approach too: if each sub-project genuinely carries a separate, independent completion obligation with no commercially relevant shared logic, standalone reporting may be entirely appropriate for THEIR own contractual reporting – but conflating 'contractually separate obligations' with 'logically independent for CPM purposes' is the trap, since the two are not the same thing when real cross-project dependencies exist.
reasoning: Program-level critical path can legitimately pass through more than one contractually distinct sub-project; excluding cross-project logic from the calculation produces float figures that are internally consistent but describe a hypothetical disconnected program, not the real one.
commonMistakes: Assuming standalone project scheduling is always wrong or always right, rather than depending on whether real cross-project logic exists and matters.
Not recommending a periodic combined-schedule run alongside the standalone reporting, treating it as an either/or choice.
Failing to acknowledge any legitimate use case for the JV partner's approach.
redFlags: Cannot articulate the mechanism by which independent scheduling understates program-level float.
Recommends forcing the JV partner to abandon standalone reporting entirely rather than adding combined reporting alongside it.
p6Checks: Open all logically linked sub-projects together in one session and schedule with cross-project relationships honored ('Ignore relationships to and from other projects' unchecked).
Compare Total Float and critical path results between the combined run and each standalone run to quantify the understatement.
Confirm which cross-project relationships genuinely exist and are being honored versus dangling/external constraints substituting for them when projects are scheduled alone.

Not checking the code's scope (Global/EPS/Project) before diagnosing the cause as a copy/paste bug.
Recreating the value manually in Project B without addressing the root cause for future copies.

skill: Explaining how choosing Longest Path versus Total Float <= 0 changes which activities are flagged critical, and why the two sets can diverge
scenario: A metro station schedule has two finish milestones: 'Station Substantial Completion' (the true project end, driven by the longest logic chain) and 'Interim Utility Diversion Complete' (an interim milestone with its own Finish-On-or-Before constraint set two weeks earlier than its logic-calculated date, creating a locally negative-float pocket on that side chain). Under 'Define critical activities as: Total Float <= 0 days,' both the true driving chain to Station Substantial Completion AND the interim utility diversion chain show as Critical. Under 'Longest Path,' only the true driving chain to Station Substantial Completion is flagged Critical.
question: Explain why these two critical-activity definitions produce a different set of 'critical' activities here, and which one you would rely on to communicate 'the' critical path to the project team.
expectedAnswer: Total Float <= 0 flags EVERY activity whose float is zero or negative, regardless of which end point or constraint drove that float to zero – here, both the true project-driving chain and the interim utility diversion chain (made artificially negative-float by its own tight constraint) qualify, because both mathematically satisfy Total Float <= 0. Longest Path instead traces the single, actual longest continuous chain of driving relationships from project start to the project finish, which here is only the chain to Station Substantial Completion – the interim milestone's own locally-critical side chain is excluded because it isn't part of that one longest chain, even though its float also happens to be zero or negative. For communicating 'the' critical path driving overall project completion, Longest Path is generally the more reliable single answer, since Total Float <= 0 can flag multiple, structurally unrelated critical-looking chains driven by different constraints, which is confusing to a team without further explanation.
strongAnswer: Notes both views are legitimately used together in practice: Total Float <= 0 (or a wider threshold) is useful for surfacing ALL near-zero-float risk areas across the whole schedule, including the interim milestone's own risk, while Longest Path answers the specific question of what one chain determines overall project completion.
explanation: The two settings answer different questions – 'which activities currently have no or negative float' versus 'which single chain of driving logic determines the project finish' – and they only necessarily coincide when there is exactly one governing constraint in the whole schedule.
reasoning: Multiple constraints (here, the interim milestone's own Finish-On-or-Before date) can independently drive separate chains to zero or negative float without those chains being part of the one true longest path to project completion, which is exactly what creates the divergence between the two definitions.
commonMistakes: Assuming Total Float <= 0 and Longest Path always identify the same activities.
Not recognizing that an interim milestone's own constraint can create a second, structurally separate 'critical-looking' chain.
Reporting 'the critical path' without specifying which definition was used to identify it.
redFlags: Cannot explain any mechanism by which two critical-activity definitions could disagree on the same schedule.

Activities view – filter/color activities by the Critical flag under each setting and compare which activities are included.

subcategory: Schedule Options – Total Float Calculation Basis
skill: Diagnosing an activity whose Total Float value depends on whether it is computed from Start Float, Finish Float, or the smaller of the two, on a multi-calendar schedule
scenario: On an LNG terminal project with several different working calendars in use (a 7-day/week calendar for marine works, a 6-day/week calendar for onshore civil, and a 5-day/week calendar for engineering/office activities), activity 'Submit As-Built Drawings – Jetty Package' shows Total Float of 9 days when the project's schedule option 'Compute Total Float as' is set to 'Start Float,' but only 3 days when set to 'Finish Float.' The planning lead is unsure which is correct and which to report.
question: How can the same activity have two different Total Float values depending only on this option, and how would you decide which basis to use for reporting on a project with mixed calendars like this?
explanation: In a schedule where an activity's own calendar differs from the calendar(s) governing the relationship chain that constrains it, the amount of float measured at the activity's Start can differ from the float measured at its Finish, because each is effectively counted across working periods of potentially different calendars along the path to the late date. 'Compute Total Float as' lets the project choose Start Float, Finish Float, or the smaller (more conservative) of the two as the reported Total Float value. On a genuinely mixed-calendar schedule like this one, using the smaller of Start and Finish Float is generally the safer, more conservative basis for reporting float and identifying risk, since it never overstates the float actually available on a mixed-calendar path.
reasoning: Total Float is fundamentally a measure of how much an activity's dates can slip before affecting a downstream constraint; when different portions of that measurement pass through different calendars, the Start-anchored and Finish-anchored versions of that measurement are not guaranteed to be numerically equal, and the option controls which (or the more conservative combination) P6 reports as 'the' Total Float.
commonMistakes: Assuming Start Float and Finish Float must always be equal and treating a discrepancy as a data error.
Picking whichever basis produces the more favorable (larger) float number without justification.
Not disclosing which basis is in use when reporting float figures to stakeholders.
redFlags: Reports the larger of the two figures without understanding why they differ, purely because it looks better.

Confirm which calendars are actually assigned to the activity itself versus the activities/relationships along its driving path.

subcategory: Schedule Options – Calendar for Relationship Lag
skill: Explaining how the calendar used to interpret relationship lag changes calculated dates when predecessor and successor use different calendars
scenario: Activity 'Backfill Trench – Section 9' (6-day/week calendar) has a Finish-to-Start relationship with 5 days of lag to its successor 'Density Testing' (5-day/week calendar). The project's schedule option 'Calendar for scheduling Relationship Lag' is currently set to 'Predecessor Activity Calendar.'
question: Explain which calendar actually governs how the 5-day lag is counted here, and what would change about the successor's calculated start date if the option were instead set to the Successor Activity Calendar.
expectedAnswer: With the option set to Predecessor Activity Calendar, the 5-day lag between the backfill's finish and density testing's start is counted using the 6-day/week backfill calendar's working periods. If it were instead set to Successor Activity Calendar, the same 5-unit lag would be counted against the 5-day/week testing calendar's working periods, which spans more elapsed calendar days for 5 working periods than a 6-day-week calendar does (since a 5-day week has more non-work days), pushing the successor's calculated start later than under the predecessor-calendar option.
strongAnswer: Adds that this option applies uniformly to every relationship's lag calculation project-wide (or session-wide), so on a project with many mixed-calendar relationships, knowing which basis is active matters for correctly predicting or explaining calculated dates broadly, not just for this one relationship.
explanation: Relationship lag is stored as a duration value, but which calendar's working/non-working pattern is used to convert that duration into actual calendar time is a configurable schedule option, and predecessor and successor calendars can produce materially different elapsed spans for the same lag value.
reasoning: A fixed number of working-period lag units maps to more or fewer actual calendar days depending on how many non-working days are interspersed in the governing calendar, so choosing a calendar with fewer working days per week for the same lag value stretches out the elapsed time before the successor can start.

explanation: Use Expected Finish Dates is a schedule option that, when enabled, ties Remaining Duration calculation to a manually entered Expected Finish field rather than to whatever Remaining Duration was previously set or calculated from progress, which can produce exactly this kind of silent, no-progress-entry change purely from the Data Date advancing.
reasoning: Because the Expected Finish date itself did not change, but the Data Date did, the gap between them shrank, and with the option enabled that shrinking gap directly becomes the new Remaining Duration – a mechanism entirely independent of actual progress entry.

subcategory: Schedule Options – Make Open-Ended Activities Critical
skill: Explaining what the Make Open-Ended Activities Critical schedule option does and diagnosing its effect on an activity with no successor
scenario: A planner notices activity 'Procure Long-Lead Switchgear' has no successor relationship at all (an open end) and, despite what looks like generous float based on its position in the schedule, is flagged Critical. The project has the schedule option 'Make open-ended activities critical' enabled.
question: Is it possible for an activity with no successor to be flagged Critical purely because of this setting, even without any tight constraint or logic actually driving it? Explain the mechanism, and state whether you would recommend leaving this option enabled.
expectedAnswer: Yes. 'Make open-ended activities critical' is a schedule option that, when enabled, forces any activity with an open end (most commonly a missing successor, but also a missing predecessor) to be flagged Critical regardless of its calculated float, specifically to make dangling or incomplete logic highly visible rather than letting it hide behind an artificially generous float value. An open-ended activity without this option can otherwise show large, misleading float simply because nothing downstream is constraining it, which understates real schedule risk if that missing logic was accidental. Leaving this option enabled is generally sound schedule-quality practice, since it surfaces logic gaps loudly instead of letting them pass silently – the fix in a case like this is usually to add the missing successor relationship (tying procurement to whatever activity actually needs the switchgear delivered), not to disable the option.
strongAnswer: Notes a complementary practice is a dedicated open-ends filter/report reviewed as part of routine schedule quality review, so open ends are still caught by process even if this option is ever disabled for some reason on a particular project.
explanation: This option exists specifically because an open-ended activity's float is otherwise computed as if the schedule simply ends there with no further constraint, which is almost always a modeling gap rather than a genuine feature of the real work plan.
reasoning: Without any successor, the backward pass has nothing downstream to constrain the activity's late dates within the normal logic network, so float would otherwise be calculated against the project's overall end date in a way that can look artificially generous; forcing Critical status overrides that misleading appearance.
commonMistakes: Assuming the Critical flag here must indicate a genuine tight logic constraint rather than the open-end override.
Recommending the option be disabled simply because the resulting Critical flags are inconvenient, without recognizing what they're protecting against.
redFlags: Recommends disabling the option purely to stop 'noisy' Critical flags without checking whether real open ends exist first.

skill: Identifying which of several converging predecessors is the driving relationship determining a successor's early start
scenario: Activity 'Pour Structural Slab – Level 5' has three Finish-to-Start predecessors: 'Install Rebar – Level 5,' whose finish would put the slab's early start at day 120; 'Formwork Complete – Level 5,' whose finish would put it at day 115; and 'MEP Sleeves Installed – Level 5,' whose finish would put it at day 108.
