question: Which of the three predecessors is the driving relationship, and how do you know without needing P6 to explicitly label it for you?
expectedAnswer: 'Install Rebar – Level 5' is the driving predecessor. For a set of Finish-to-Start predecessors converging on one successor, the forward pass takes the LATEST of all the individually-calculated early start dates each predecessor relationship would impose, and day 120 (from rebar) is later than both day 115 (formwork) and day 108 (MEP sleeves) – so rebar's finish is the one actually constraining the slab pour's start. The other two have slack relative to this successor and are not driving it, even though they remain legitimate, already-satisfied predecessors.
strongAnswer: Notes this can be confirmed directly in P6 without manual reasoning by checking the Driving flag/column P6 calculates and displays on each relationship in the Relationships tab, rather than requiring the planner to infer it by comparing dates by hand every time.
explanation: Among multiple FS predecessors feeding one successor, the successor's early start is governed by whichever predecessor relationship produces the latest resulting date; that is the definition of the driving relationship in this configuration.
reasoning: The forward pass logic for a converging set of predecessors takes the maximum (latest) of the candidate early dates each relationship proposes, since the successor cannot logically start before ANY of its predecessors' requirements are satisfied.
commonMistakes: Assuming the predecessor listed first in the Relationships tab is automatically the driving one.
Assuming all three predecessors are equally 'driving' because they are all legitimate FS relationships.
Picking the predecessor with the longest duration rather than the one producing the latest resulting date.
redFlags: Cannot correctly identify the driving predecessor from the given dates.

skill: Explaining why an activity's Total Float alone does not reveal which of its several predecessor relationships is actually driving it

subcategory: Negative Float – Must Finish By Project Date

scenario: You are the Project Controls Manager on a hotel renovation project with a contractual completion date entered as the project's 'Must Finish By' date. question: How do you explain the -27 days to the GM, and what is your recommended path forward, distinguishing the technical schedule finding from the contractual/commercial question of what happens next?
expectedAnswer: The -27 days is a technical CPM statement: based on current logic, durations, and progress, the project as currently planned will finish 27 days later than the contractual Must Finish By date if nothing changes; it is not itself a statement about who is responsible or what remedy applies. Recommended path forward: identify and review the driving path causing the 27-day gap via Trace Logic (are there recoverable delays through acceleration or resequencing, or float-consuming logic worth revisiting), quantify realistic recovery options and their cost, and separately work with the commercial/contracts team to determine whether any portion of the 27 days traces to owner-caused or excusable events that could support an EOT request – these are two parallel workstreams, technical recovery planning and contractual entitlement assessment, and the GM needs both, not just the schedule number.
strongAnswer: Cautions against conflating 'we are 27 days behind the contractual date' with 'we will definitely absorb 27 days of liquidated damages exposure,' since entitlement depends on the contract terms, causation, and notice provisions, and some of the 27 days could turn out to be excusable.
expertAnswer: Adds the governance point that a material Must Finish By shortfall like this should be formally documented and escalated (not just described verbally), given the potential liquidated damages exposure, and that the finding should trigger the recovery-planning and entitlement-assessment workstreams promptly rather than waiting for the next monthly cycle.
explanation: Separating the technical schedule finding from the contractual/commercial response is the core competency being tested; treating -27 days as automatically meaning 'contractor is 27 days liable' or automatically meaning 'nothing to worry about, it will sort itself out' are both wrong.
reasoning: CPM float is a mathematical statement about the current logic network relative to a fixed date; entitlement, liability, and recovery feasibility require separate technical (driving-path/recovery) and contractual (causation, notice, excusability) analysis layered on top of that number.
commonMistakes: Presenting -27 days to the GM as a simple, single-cause number without breaking down the driving path.
Immediately assuming full contractor liability for all 27 days without any entitlement analysis.
Proposing recovery measures without first identifying the actual driving path causing the gap.
redFlags: Cannot distinguish the technical schedule finding from the contractual entitlement question.
Treats the number as purely a reporting problem rather than a planning and commercial issue requiring parallel action.
p6Checks: Project Details > Dates tab – confirm the Must Finish By date matches the actual contractual completion date.
Trace Logic / Longest Path on the driving finish milestone to identify the actual driving chain producing the 27-day gap.
Review whether any portion of the driving delay traces to owner-caused or excusable events versus contractor-caused activities.

skill: Diagnosing negative float on a project caused entirely by an external predecessor in a separate, linked project
scenario: The 'MEP Fit-Out' project shows -9 days Total Float on its driving path, even though every activity and relationship WITHIN 'MEP Fit-Out' itself, reviewed exhaustively, appears logically sound with no unusual constraints. 'MEP Fit-Out' has one external Finish-to-Start predecessor relationship, 'Building Envelope Watertight,' which belongs to a separate project, 'Main Structure,' currently running 9 days behind its own baseline.
question: Explain how a project with entirely clean internal logic can still show negative float, and what you would check to confirm the cross-project cause before proposing any recovery plan within MEP Fit-Out itself.
expectedAnswer: Negative float is calculated relative to whatever constrains an activity's late dates, which for MEP Fit-Out's earliest activities is the external predecessor 'Building Envelope Watertight' in 'Main Structure.' If that external predecessor's own forecast finish has slipped, and cross-project relationships are being honored (both projects open together, with 'Ignore relationships to and from other projects' disabled), the delay propagates directly into MEP Fit-Out's early dates, and combined with a downstream fixed constraint or Must Finish By date on MEP Fit-Out itself, produces negative float even though nothing internal to MEP Fit-Out is at fault. To confirm before proposing any recovery plan, verify that Main Structure's slip on 'Building Envelope Watertight' matches the magnitude of MEP Fit-Out's negative float, and check that both projects were open together, with cross-project relationships honored, when this figure was calculated – a recovery plan aimed at MEP Fit-Out's own activities would be the wrong target if the true cause sits entirely upstream in a different project.
strongAnswer: Notes the practical implication clearly: any recovery or acceleration effort should logically target Main Structure's envelope completion first, since accelerating MEP Fit-Out's own activities cannot address a delay whose root cause is external to that project.
explanation: Float and critical path calculations depend on the complete logic network constraining an activity, which can legitimately extend outside the project being examined when genuine cross-project relationships exist.
reasoning: A project's internal logic can be entirely sound while still inheriting negative float from an external constraint, because Total Float is a property of the whole connected network relative to a governing date, not of any one project's activities in isolation.
commonMistakes: Assuming clean internal logic rules out negative float entirely.
Searching exhaustively within MEP Fit-Out for a cause that doesn't exist there.
Proposing a recovery plan focused on MEP Fit-Out's own activities without first confirming the cross-project cause.
redFlags: Cannot conceive of an external, cross-project cause for negative float and insists the cause must be internal.
p6Checks: Open both 'Main Structure' and 'MEP Fit-Out' together and confirm 'Ignore relationships to and from other projects' is disabled when calculating the reported float.
Relationships tab on MEP Fit-Out's earliest activities – confirm the external predecessor 'Building Envelope Watertight' and compare its current forecast finish against its baseline.
Trace Logic from MEP Fit-Out's negative-float driving activity back through the external relationship into Main Structure to confirm the causal chain.

followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests communication judgment when a technical finding shifts responsibility away from the party who might naturally be blamed.

skill: Weighing genuine recovery planning against a cosmetic constraint edit as the correct response to reported negative float
scenario: A junior planner reports negative float of -11 days on the driving path of a power plant commissioning schedule and proposes simply changing the Mandatory Finish constraint on the final milestone to a Finish-On-or-Before constraint (or removing it entirely) so the float 'goes back to positive' before this month's client report is issued.
question: As the planning manager reviewing this before issue, do you approve this fix? Walk through how you would actually determine the right response to this negative float.
explanation: Do not approve simply changing or removing the constraint to make the float number look better without first understanding why the milestone has a Mandatory Finish constraint in the first place, very likely tied to a genuine contractual completion date or hard external commitment – loosening it doesn't change the underlying reality that the logic-calculated finish is 11 days later than required, it only stops the schedule from reporting that fact. The correct process: (1) confirm the constraint is legitimate and still required with contracts/commercial; if so, it stays; (2) identify the actual driving path causing the -11 days via Trace Logic/Longest Path; (3) determine whether the negative float stems from a genuine logic/calendar error worth correcting (an unnecessarily conservative lag, a misassigned calendar) versus real remaining work that genuinely takes that long; (4) if it's genuine, develop and cost real recovery options (resequencing, added shifts/resources, method changes) and report the negative float transparently alongside the recovery plan, rather than making the number disappear cosmetically.
reasoning: Negative float is a symptom of an underlying mismatch between required and calculated completion; editing the constraint that reveals that mismatch treats the symptom's visibility, not the mismatch itself, and can constitute a serious schedule-integrity and disclosure problem if reported to a client.
commonMistakes: Treating negative float as primarily a reporting/optics problem to be resolved by adjusting a constraint.
Not distinguishing between negative float caused by a genuine data/logic error versus one reflecting real remaining-work duration.
Skipping the step of confirming whether the constraint itself is still contractually valid.
redFlags: Approves removing or loosening the constraint purely to make the reported number look better without investigating the underlying cause.
Cannot distinguish negative float indicating a real problem from one caused by a data/logic error.
p6Checks: Activity's Status/General tab – confirm the constraint type and date on the final milestone, and its basis (contractual date, etc.).
Trace Logic/Longest Path from the milestone to identify the actual driving path producing the -11 days.
Review the driving path's logic, calendars, and durations for genuine errors versus real remaining-work duration.
If genuine, develop and cost recovery options rather than editing the constraint.

followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate can address the underlying communication concern constructively instead of dismissing it or capitulating to it.

skill: Diagnosing why the driving predecessor to a milestone changed between two consecutive schedule updates even though overall float barely moved
scenario: Last month, Trace Logic on milestone 'Substation Energization' showed the driving chain running through 'Deliver Transformer T-2' (a procurement activity). This month, after both the transformer delivery and several other predecessor activities progressed, Trace Logic now shows the driving chain running through a completely different activity, 'Complete Protection Relay Testing,' even though the milestone's Total Float barely changed, from -2 days to -3 days.
question: Is it possible for the driving predecessor to change from one update to the next even while overall float barely moves, and what does that tell you (or not tell you) about which activity to focus recovery efforts on this month?
explanation: Yes, this is possible and is a normal feature of CPM networks with multiple paths of similar length converging on the same successor: once 'Deliver Transformer T-2' progressed enough that its path's calculated date pulled ahead, another path, the one running through protection relay testing, became the later (driving) one, even though the two paths were close enough in length that overall float barely changed. This tells the team that recovery focus should shift THIS month to 'Complete Protection Relay Testing' and its own predecessors, since accelerating the transformer delivery chain further would no longer help the milestone date at all, even though it was the correct focus last month.
reasoning: In a network with two or more near-parallel paths of similar total length, small period-to-period changes can flip which path is momentarily the longer (driving) one, without necessarily producing a large change in the milestone's overall float, since the float is governed by the gap to the near-equally-long alternate path either way.
commonMistakes: Assuming the driving predecessor identified last month is still automatically the one to focus on this month.
Assuming a small float change means nothing structurally significant changed.
Continuing recovery efforts on the previous month's driving activity without re-verifying via Trace Logic first.
redFlags: Continues directing recovery resources at last month's driving activity without re-checking this month's actual driving chain.
p6Checks: Trace Logic on 'Substation Energization' this period versus a saved/exported version of last period's trace to directly compare the two driving chains.
Relationships tab – confirm the Driving flag has shifted to the protection relay testing predecessor this period.
Before committing recovery resources, re-verify the CURRENT driving chain rather than assuming it matches last period's.

followUpQuestions.prompt: How would you explain this shift to a site team that spent significant effort accelerating the transformer delivery last month, only to be told that's no longer the constraint?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests communication judgment when a legitimate prior recovery effort is superseded by new information, without undermining confidence in the schedule.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Would you expect this kind of driving-chain shift to happen more or less often on a schedule with many near-parallel paths of similar length versus one with a single dominant critical path?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate generalizes the mechanism to network structure characteristics.

skill: Calculating the planned cost allocated to a specific period from a defined resource curve's percentage distribution
scenario: An activity assignment has Budgeted Cost of $600,000 spread across a 10-week duration using a curve defined across five two-week buckets covering the full duration, with the following period allocations: Weeks 1-2: 30%, Weeks 3-4: 25%, Weeks 5-6: 20%, Weeks 7-8: 15%, Weeks 9-10: 10% (summing to 100%).
question: What is the planned cost allocated to Weeks 5-6 under this curve?
explanation: Weeks 5-6 is allocated 20% of the total Budgeted Cost: 20% x $600,000 = $120,000.
reasoning: A resource/cost curve redistributes the fixed total Budgeted Cost across the assignment's duration according to defined period percentages that must sum to 100%; the dollar amount for any given period is simply that period's percentage of the total.
commonMistakes: Assuming cost is spread evenly (linearly) despite a curve being defined.
Calculating cumulative-to-date cost rather than the amount for just Weeks 5-6.
Using the wrong period's percentage from the table.
p6Checks: Enterprise Data > Curves – open the curve definition and confirm the percentage assigned to each period bucket sums to 100%.
Activity's Resources tab – confirm the Curve field references this specific curve on the assignment.
Resource Usage Spreadsheet, set to show Cost by period, to directly read the calculated per-period planned cost and cross-check the manual calculation.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What would the cumulative planned cost be through the end of Week 6?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate can extend the single-period calculation to a cumulative PV figure (30%+25%+20% = 75% x $600,000 = $450,000).

subcategory: Comprehensive Diagnosis – Out-of-Sequence Progress, Retained Logic, and Negative Float
skill: Integrating out-of-sequence progress, Retained Logic behavior, and negative float diagnosis into one coherent troubleshooting narrative
scenario: A desalination plant EPC project's monthly update shows: (1) the Schedule Log reports 22 activities with out-of-sequence progress, and Retained Logic is the active Out-of-Sequence Progress option; (2) the project's finish milestone, which carried a Must Finish By-driven negative float of -5 days last month, now shows -19 days this month; (3) the independent field progress report confirms the project is, if anything, slightly ahead on physical completion percentage versus last month across most disciplines.
question: Walk through how you would investigate this apparent contradiction, float dropping sharply despite physical progress reportedly being ahead, integrating what you know about out-of-sequence progress, Retained Logic, and negative float, and describe the order in which you would check things.
expectedAnswer: Start by not assuming the two signals are actually in real conflict, since they measure different things: physical percent complete measures the VOLUME of work done, while Total Float on the finish milestone measures the current forecast of the REMAINING, unexecuted logic-driven chain relative to the Must Finish By date. Investigation order: (1) use Trace Logic on the finish milestone to identify this month's actual driving chain and compare it against last month's – has the driving path itself shifted; (2) for the 22 out-of-sequence activities, check whether any lie on or near the current driving chain – under Retained Logic, an OOS activity's REMAINING work stays tied to its unfinished predecessor's requirement, so if several of these OOS activities' governing predecessors themselves slipped this period, the retained-logic-constrained remaining work could be pushing the driving chain's forecast later even while headline percent-complete on those same activities looks favorable; (3) confirm the Must Finish By date itself hasn't changed, ruling out that as a separate cause; (4) once the mechanism is confirmed, distinguish which portion of the 14-day float deterioration (from -5 to -19) is attributable to genuine remaining-duration/retained-logic effects versus any other change (added scope, constraint edits, calendar changes) by also reviewing what changed since last month, for example via Claim Digger, before concluding.
strongAnswer: Adds that this integrated diagnosis should be documented clearly for the client/PM specifically because 'ahead on physical progress but float collapsing' is exactly the kind of result that looks paradoxical and can undermine confidence in the schedule if it isn't explained mechanically rather than dismissed or oversimplified.
expertAnswer: Notes the governance angle: a 14-day single-month deterioration on a schedule already carrying negative float against a Must Finish By date is a serious commercial signal, given likely liquidated damages exposure, that should trigger prompt escalation and a documented recovery-options review in parallel with the technical diagnosis, not just a technical explanation delivered after the fact.
explanation: This scenario requires combining several distinct P6 mechanics, out-of-sequence progress, Retained Logic's effect on remaining duration, driving-chain identification, and negative float interpretation, into a single coherent investigation rather than treating each as an isolated fact.
reasoning: Percent complete and Total Float are fundamentally different measurements (volume of work done versus forecast risk to a governing date); a schedule can be genuinely ahead on the first while deteriorating on the second when the specific mechanics of Retained Logic on out-of-sequence activities interact with a predecessor slip on the current driving chain.
commonMistakes: Treating the physical-progress-ahead and float-collapsing signals as necessarily contradictory rather than investigating the mechanism connecting them.
Investigating the 22 out-of-sequence activities as a flat list without first identifying which ones are actually relevant to the current driving chain.
Concluding a cause without checking for other contributing changes (constraint, calendar, scope) since the prior period.
redFlags: Dismisses the field progress report as simply wrong without investigating the mechanical explanation.
Cannot connect Retained Logic's effect on remaining duration to the driving-chain deterioration at all.
Fails to flag the commercial/LD urgency of a 14-day single-month deterioration against a Must Finish By date.
p6Checks: Trace Logic on the finish milestone, this month versus last month, to compare driving chains.
Activities view filtered to Out-of-Sequence Progress – cross-reference against the current driving chain to see which OOS activities are actually relevant.
Confirm Retained Logic is still the active Out-of-Sequence Progress option, unchanged from last period.
Project Details > Dates tab – confirm the Must Finish By date itself hasn't changed.
Claim Digger comparing this month's and last month's XER to catch any other logic, constraint, or calendar changes contributing to the float deterioration.
